lphy-01-c1.text: Johann-Mattis List, Shijulal Nelson-Sathi, Hans Geisler, William Martin (2014). Networks of lexical borrowing and lateral gene transfer in language and genome evolution. BioEssays.
lphy-01-c1.quote: Schleicher himself adopted the idea from a colleague, the Czech linguist František Ladislav Čelakovský (1759–1852), whose posthumously published lectures contain an early tree diagram of the Slavic languages
lphy-01-c1.claim: He may have borrowed the picture from a colleague, the Czech linguist František Ladislav Čelakovský, whose lectures, published after his death, contain an early tree diagram of the Slavic languages.

lphy-01-c1.text: Johann-Mattis List, Shijulal Nelson-Sathi, Hans Geisler, William Martin (2014). Networks of lexical borrowing and lateral gene transfer in language and genome evolution. BioEssays.
lphy-01-c1.quote: Schleicher was very interested in biology, especially botany, and in his work we find many passages where he compares languages with organisms
lphy-01-c1.claim: Schleicher was very interested in biology, especially botany, and he liked to compare languages with organisms that pass through birth, youth, old age and death.

lphy-01-c1.text: Russell D. Gray, David Bryant, Simon J. Greenhill (2010). On the shape and fabric of human history. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B.
lphy-01-c1.quote: The influential American anthropologist Kroeber (1948) explicitly contrasted Darwin's idea of a ‘tree of life’ with that of a ‘tree of cultures’.
lphy-01-c1.claim: As early as 1948 the American anthropologist Kroeber explicitly contrasted Darwin's idea of a tree of life with that of a tree of cultures

lphy-01-c2.text: Johann-Mattis List, Jananan Sylvestre Pathmanathan, Philippe Lopez, Eric Bapteste (2016). Unity and disunity in evolutionary sciences: process-based analogies open common research avenues for biology and linguistics. Biology Direct.
lphy-01-c2.quote: In linguistics, approaches for subgrouping based on shared innovations (or shared derived characters) date back to the end of the 19th century
lphy-01-c2.claim: Subgrouping by shared innovations dates back to the end of the nineteenth century.

lphy-01-c2.text: Laurent Sagart, Guillaume Jacques, Yunfan Lai, Robin J. Ryder, Valentin Thouzeau, Simon J. Greenhill, Johann-Mattis List (2019). Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-01-c2.quote: the commonalities in verbal morphology adduced by these authors to support these subgroups are more likely to reflect a combination of retentions from a common ancestor and parallel innovations
lphy-01-c2.claim: When Laurent Sagart and colleagues built dated trees for Sino-Tibetan in 2019, they concluded that similarities in verb morphology once offered as evidence for certain subgroups more likely reflect a mix of retentions and parallel innovations.

lphy-01-c2.text: Simon J. Greenhill, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray (2010). How accurate and robust are the phylogenetic estimates of Austronesian language relationships?. PLoS ONE.
lphy-01-c2.quote: the traditional subgroupings defined largely on the basis of phonological evidence such as the loss of the Proto-Oceanic uvular trill *R in the Central Pacific subgroup
lphy-01-c2.claim: In Austronesian, the Central Pacific subgroup is defined partly by the loss of the Proto-Oceanic uvular trill *R, and Central-Eastern Malayo-Polynesian partly by the lowering of high vowels in certain morphemes.

lphy-01-c2.text: Simon J. Greenhill, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray (2010). How accurate and robust are the phylogenetic estimates of Austronesian language relationships?. PLoS ONE.
lphy-01-c2.quote: We reported that our analyses supported 26 of the 34 main Austronesian subgroups proposed by historical linguists
lphy-01-c2.claim: supported 26 of the 34 main subgroups proposed by historical linguists

lphy-01-c3.text: Johann-Mattis List, Shijulal Nelson-Sathi, Hans Geisler, William Martin (2014). Networks of lexical borrowing and lateral gene transfer in language and genome evolution. BioEssays.
lphy-01-c3.quote: emphasizing that languages diverge gradually while at the same time mutually influencing each other
lphy-01-c3.claim: Before Schmidt, Hugo Schuchardt had already stressed that languages diverge gradually while still influencing each other.

lphy-01-c3.text: Johann-Mattis List, Shijulal Nelson-Sathi, Hans Geisler, William Martin (2014). Networks of lexical borrowing and lateral gene transfer in language and genome evolution. BioEssays.
lphy-01-c3.quote: In text books on historical linguistics, both the tree and the wave theory are usually introduced as two complementary models, each of which only depicts one aspect of language history
lphy-01-c3.claim: Textbooks now usually present the tree and the wave as two complementary models, each showing one side of language history.

lphy-01-c3.text: Russell D. Gray, David Bryant, Simon J. Greenhill (2010). On the shape and fabric of human history. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B.
lphy-01-c3.quote: On the basis of linguistic evidence, Pawley (1996) has argued that the settlement of Polynesia involved the establishment and break-up of a series of dialect chains.
lphy-01-c3.claim: Working from linguistic evidence, Pawley argued in 1996 that the settlement of Polynesia involved the establishment and break-up of a whole series of dialect chains.

lphy-01-c3.text: Russell D. Gray, David Bryant, Simon J. Greenhill (2010). On the shape and fabric of human history. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B.
lphy-01-c3.quote: Sranan stands out as having the highest taxon-specific scores reflecting its hybrid history (delta score = 0.29, Q-residual = 0.05)
lphy-01-c3.claim: The set scored 0.23 overall, and Sranan, with its mixed history, scored highest at 0.29.

lphy-01-c3.text: Russell D. Gray, David Bryant, Simon J. Greenhill (2010). On the shape and fabric of human history. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B.
lphy-01-c3.quote: the voyaging skills of the Polynesians meant that the substantial ocean distances were not necessarily a barrier to ongoing contact
lphy-01-c3.claim: The voyaging skills of the Polynesians meant that ocean distances were no barrier to ongoing contact.

lphy-02-c1.text: Menghan Zhang, Tao Gong (2016). How many is enough? Statistical principles for lexicostatistics. Frontiers in Psychology.
Menghan Zhang, Tao Gong (2016). How many is enough? Statistical principles for lexicostatistics. Frontiers in Psychology.
lphy-02-c1.quote: note that about 10% of the Swadesh 100-word list are still prone to borrowing
lphy-02-c1.claim: The resistance is only relative: about 10% of the Swadesh 100-word list is still prone to borrowing.

lphy-02-c1.text: Menghan Zhang, Tao Gong (2016). How many is enough? Statistical principles for lexicostatistics. Frontiers in Psychology.
lphy-02-c1.quote: Some of these lists contain 40 (Holman et al., 2008), 35 (Starostin, 2000), 33 (Baxter and Ramer, 2000), or only 15 (Dolgopolsky, 1986) concepts.
lphy-02-c1.claim: later scholars proposed even shorter lists, of 40, 35, 33 or only 15 concepts, chosen largely by linguistic intuition and experience

lphy-02-c2.text: Jacques B. M. Guy (1982). Bases for new methods in glottochronology. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
lphy-02-c2.quote: relying on a retention rate of 86% per millennium (the one generally used for the Swadesh 100-item wordlist)
lphy-02-c2.claim: The constant generally used for the 100-word list was a retention rate of 86% per millennium.

lphy-02-c2.text: Jacques B. M. Guy (1982). Bases for new methods in glottochronology. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
lphy-02-c2.quote: one would confidently predict that their most likely percentage of shared cognates should be around 73.96%
lphy-02-c2.claim: Two languages that split 1,000 years ago should share about 0.86 × 0.86, or 74%, of their list.

lphy-02-c2.text: Jacques B. M. Guy (1982). Bases for new methods in glottochronology. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
lphy-02-c2.quote: It is quite unreasonable to hold that language families allow their members to split only at those times when their average rates of drift happen to be equal to a certain constant value.
lphy-02-c2.claim: it would be quite unreasonable for every language family to split only when its average rate happened to equal one constant value

lphy-02-c3.text: Jacques B. M. Guy (1982). Bases for new methods in glottochronology. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
lphy-02-c3.quote: In 1962 Bergsland and Vogt presented conclusive evidence that retention rates could vary greatly across languages.
lphy-02-c3.claim: In 1962 Bergsland and Vogt tested glottochronology on closely related languages and dialects and found that retention rates varied enormously.

lphy-02-c3.text: Jacques B. M. Guy (1982). Bases for new methods in glottochronology. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
lphy-02-c3.quote: If however X and Y had had the bad taste of evolving at the same rates as East and West Greenlandic (53.7% and 97.2% retention per millennium respectively), they would most probably share 52.2% cognates.
lphy-02-c3.claim: One pair was East and West Greenlandic, two closely related varieties, which kept 53.7% and 97.2% of the list per millennium respectively.

lphy-02-c3.text: Jacques B. M. Guy (1982). Bases for new methods in glottochronology. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
lphy-02-c3.quote: In 1965 Dyen, James and Cole had calculated the retention rates of the individual items of a standard sample wordlist, which were also found to vary.
lphy-02-c3.claim: In 1965 Dyen, James and Cole calculated retention rates for the individual items on a standard list and found that those varied as well.

lphy-02-c3.text: Jacques B. M. Guy (1982). Bases for new methods in glottochronology. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
lphy-02-c3.quote: And after three periods of time 36.5% will be left, not 12.5%.
lphy-02-c3.claim: The real figures are 41% and 36.5%, because the slow words come to dominate what is left.

lphy-02-c3.text: Jacques B. M. Guy (1982). Bases for new methods in glottochronology. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
lphy-02-c3.quote: should have brought about drastic, if painful, revisions in the lexicostatistical method
lphy-02-c3.claim: Guy judged that Bergsland and Vogt's study should have brought about drastic, if painful, revisions in the lexicostatistical method, and that it was ignored.

lphy-03-c1.text: Russell D. Gray, Quentin D. Atkinson (2003). Language-tree divergence times support the Anatolian theory of Indo-European origin. Nature.
lphy-03-c1.quote: our analysis of a matrix of 87 languages with 2,449 lexical items produced an estimated age range for the initial Indo-European divergence
lphy-03-c1.claim: Russell Gray and Quentin Atkinson's 2003 analysis of Indo-European used a matrix of 87 languages with 2,449 lexical items coded this way.

lphy-03-c1.text: Russell D. Gray, David Bryant, Simon J. Greenhill (2010). On the shape and fabric of human history. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B.
lphy-03-c1.quote: the stochastic Dollo model developed by Nicholls & Gray (2006, 2008) in which cognates can evolve only once but be lost multiple times
lphy-03-c1.claim: a cognate can evolve only once but be lost multiple times

lphy-03-c1.text: Rebecca Grollemund, Simon Branford, Koen Bostoen, Andrew Meade, Chris Venditti, Mark Pagel (2015). Bantu expansion shows that habitat alters the route and pace of human dispersals. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-03-c1.quote: expert opinion on cognate classifications can differ (this difference also occurs in the alignment of gene sequence data where it is necessary to identify homologous genes)
lphy-03-c1.claim: Expert opinion on cognate classes can differ, much as biologists can disagree about how to align gene sequences, so careful studies rerun their analyses on alternative codings to check that the results hold.

lphy-03-c1.text: Paul Heggarty, Cormac Anderson, Matthew Scarborough, Benedict King, Remco Bouckaert, et al (2023). Language trees with sampled ancestors support a hybrid model for the origin of Indo-European languages. Science (New York, N.Y.).
lphy-03-c1.quote: Here we present an extensive database of Indo-European core vocabulary that eliminates past inconsistencies in cognate coding.
lphy-03-c1.claim: Coding problems were serious enough in Indo-European that in 2023 a team led by Paul Heggarty built a new database designed to eliminate past inconsistencies in cognate coding.

lphy-03-c2.text: Laurent Sagart, Guillaume Jacques, Yunfan Lai, Robin J. Ryder, Valentin Thouzeau, Simon J. Greenhill, Johann-Mattis List (2019). Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-03-c2.quote: For each model, we performed Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling to obtain a sample of plausible trees from the posterior distribution.
lphy-03-c2.claim: MCMC sampling is run to obtain a sample of plausible trees from the posterior distribution

lphy-03-c2.text: Simon J. Greenhill, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray (2010). How accurate and robust are the phylogenetic estimates of Austronesian language relationships?. PLoS ONE.
lphy-03-c2.quote: The age of the Austronesian language family was estimated to be approximately 5,200 years (95% highest posterior density interval, 4,750 to 5,800 years BP).
lphy-03-c2.claim: dates come as 95% highest posterior density intervals, such as 4,750–5,800 years for the Austronesian root

lphy-03-c2.text: Remco Bouckaert, Philippe Lemey, Michael Dunn, Simon J. Greenhill, Alexander V. Alekseyenko, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray, Marc A. Suchard, Quentin D. Atkinson (2012). Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family. Science.
lphy-03-c2.quote: A BF of 5–20 is taken as substantial support, over 20 as strong support and BFs greater than 100 are considered decisive
lphy-03-c2.claim: On the scale used by Remco Bouckaert's team, a Bayes factor of 5–20 is taken as substantial support, over 20 as strong support, and over 100 as decisive.

lphy-03-c3.text: Laurent Sagart, Guillaume Jacques, Yunfan Lai, Robin J. Ryder, Valentin Thouzeau, Simon J. Greenhill, Johann-Mattis List (2019). Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-03-c3.quote: We specified calibrations as follows: Old Chinese, [2,800 to 2,300] yBP, in a uniform prior; Old Burmese, 800 yBP; Old Tibetan, 1,200 yBP; and Tangut, 900 yBP
lphy-03-c3.claim: For their 2019 study of Sino-Tibetan, Sagart and colleagues used the dates of the earliest texts: Old Chinese at 2,800–2,300 years before present, Old Tibetan at 1,200, Tangut at 900 and Old Burmese at 800.

lphy-03-c3.text: Simon J. Greenhill, Chieh-Hsi Wu, Xia Hua, Michael Dunn, Stephen C. Levinson, Russell D. Gray (2017). Evolutionary dynamics of language systems. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-03-c3.quote: These calibrations were the following: (i) Proto-Oceanic (mean of 3,300 y, SD = 100 y)
lphy-03-c3.claim: Austronesian studies use dates for reconstructed ancestors, placing Proto-Oceanic around 3,300 years ago and Proto-Austronesian around 5,200, each with a stated uncertainty.

lphy-03-c3.text: Simon J. Greenhill, Chieh-Hsi Wu, Xia Hua, Michael Dunn, Stephen C. Levinson, Russell D. Gray (2017). Evolutionary dynamics of language systems. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-03-c3.quote: The AICM indicated that the best-fitting model for the rates comparison was a relaxed clock along with a log-normally distributed base measure of the Dirichlet process prior
lphy-03-c3.claim: When Greenhill and colleagues compared clock models for 81 Austronesian languages in 2017, relaxed clocks fitted far better than strict ones.

lphy-03-c3.text: Paul Heggarty (2013). Ultraconserved words and Eurasiatic? The "faces in the fire" of language prehistory. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-03-c3.quote: Pagel et al.’s dating is based on just two calibration points, and neither is historically known; rather, they are just hypothetical matches with archaeology.
lphy-03-c3.claim: Heggarty objected that one deep-time study rested on just two calibration points, neither historically known, only hypothetical matches with archaeology.

lphy-03-c3.text: Laurent Sagart, Guillaume Jacques, Yunfan Lai, Robin J. Ryder, Valentin Thouzeau, Simon J. Greenhill, Johann-Mattis List (2019). Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-03-c3.quote: Our findings point to Sino-Tibetan originating with north Chinese millet farmers around 7200 B.P.
lphy-03-c3.claim: The Sino-Tibetan trees, for their part, placed that family's origin with north Chinese millet farmers around 7,200 years ago.

lphy-04-c1.text: Russell D. Gray, Quentin D. Atkinson (2003). Language-tree divergence times support the Anatolian theory of Indo-European origin. Nature.
lphy-04-c1.quote: The origin of the Indo-European language family is “the most intensively studied, yet still most recalcitrant, problem of historical linguistics”
lphy-04-c1.claim: The origin of Indo-European has been called "the most intensively studied, yet still most recalcitrant, problem of historical linguistics".

lphy-04-c1.text: Russell D. Gray, Quentin D. Atkinson (2003). Language-tree divergence times support the Anatolian theory of Indo-European origin. Nature.
lphy-04-c1.quote: In striking agreement with the Anatolian hypothesis, our analysis of a matrix of 87 languages with 2,449 lexical items produced an estimated age range for the initial Indo-European divergence of between 7,800 and 9,800 years bp.
lphy-04-c1.claim: Their analysis produced an estimated age range for the initial Indo-European divergence of between 7,800 and 9,800 years ago, in what they called striking agreement with the Anatolian hypothesis.

lphy-04-c1.text: Russell D. Gray, Quentin D. Atkinson (2003). Language-tree divergence times support the Anatolian theory of Indo-European origin. Nature.
lphy-04-c1.quote: These results were robust to changes in coding procedures, calibration points, rooting of the trees and priors in the bayesian analysis.
lphy-04-c1.claim: The results were robust to changes in coding procedures, calibration points, the rooting of the trees and the priors.

lphy-04-c2.text: Remco Bouckaert, Philippe Lemey, Michael Dunn, Simon J. Greenhill, Alexander V. Alekseyenko, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray, Marc A. Suchard, Quentin D. Atkinson (2012). Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family. Science.
lphy-04-c2.quote: We use this approach to analyze a data set of basic vocabulary terms and geographic range assignments for 103 ancient and contemporary Indo-European languages
lphy-04-c2.claim: The team adapted it to basic vocabulary and geographic ranges for 103 ancient and contemporary Indo-European languages.

lphy-04-c2.text: Remco Bouckaert, Philippe Lemey, Michael Dunn, Simon J. Greenhill, Alexander V. Alekseyenko, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray, Marc A. Suchard, Quentin D. Atkinson (2012). Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family. Science.
lphy-04-c2.quote: timing (7,116–10,410 BP 95% highest posterior density [HPD]) of Indo-European origin is congruent with the proposal that the family began to diverge with the spread of agriculture from Anatolia
lphy-04-c2.claim: and the root's age came out at 7,116–10,410 years ago

lphy-04-c2.text: Remco Bouckaert, Philippe Lemey, Michael Dunn, Simon J. Greenhill, Alexander V. Alekseyenko, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray, Marc A. Suchard, Quentin D. Atkinson (2012). Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family. Science.
lphy-04-c2.quote: Our model correctly assigns high posterior support to the most recent common ancestor of contemporary Romance languages around Rome
lphy-04-c2.claim: The model placed the most recent common ancestor of the Romance languages around Rome, as history says it should.

lphy-04-c2.text: Remco Bouckaert, Philippe Lemey, Michael Dunn, Simon J. Greenhill, Alexander V. Alekseyenko, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray, Marc A. Suchard, Quentin D. Atkinson (2012). Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family. Science.
lphy-04-c2.quote: Celtic, Germanic, Italic, Balto-Slavic and Indo-Iranian – all emerged as distinct lineages between 4000 and 6000 years BP
lphy-04-c2.claim: In their tree, the five major subfamilies, Celtic, Germanic, Italic, Balto-Slavic and Indo-Iranian, all emerged as distinct lineages between 4,000 and 6,000 years ago, at the same time as later cultural expansions including the Kurgan one.

lphy-04-c3.text: Will Chang, Chundra Cathcart, David Hall, Andrew Garrett (2015). Ancestry-constrained phylogenetic analysis supports the Indo-European steppe hypothesis. Language.
lphy-04-c3.quote: we show that the result strongly supports the steppe hypothesis
lphy-04-c3.claim: With those constraints, the result strongly supported the steppe hypothesis.

lphy-04-c3.text: Will Chang, Chundra Cathcart, David Hall, Andrew Garrett (2015). Ancestry-constrained phylogenetic analysis supports the Indo-European steppe hypothesis. Language.
lphy-04-c3.quote: We show that lexical traits undergo recurrent evolution due to recurring patterns of semantic and morphological change.
lphy-04-c3.claim: Lexical traits recur because of recurring patterns of semantic and morphological change.

lphy-04-c3.text: Paul Heggarty (2013). Ultraconserved words and Eurasiatic? The "faces in the fire" of language prehistory. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
lphy-04-c3.quote: yields errors such as a Portuguese-Spanish split far too late, centered on AD 1500
lphy-04-c3.claim: Heggarty noted that the 2012 trees put the split between Portuguese and Spanish far too late, centred on AD 1500.

lphy-04-c3.text: Paul Heggarty, Cormac Anderson, Matthew Scarborough, Benedict King, Remco Bouckaert, et al (2023). Language trees with sampled ancestors support a hybrid model for the origin of Indo-European languages. Science (New York, N.Y.).
lphy-04-c3.quote: Ancestry-enabled phylogenetic analysis of this dataset indicates that few ancient languages are direct ancestors of modern clades and produces a root age of ~8120 yr B.P. for the family.
lphy-04-c3.claim: That analysis indicated that few ancient languages are direct ancestors of modern clades, which undercuts the case for forcing them into that role, and it put the root at about 8,120 years ago.

lphy-05-c1.text: Will Chang, Chundra Cathcart, David Hall, Andrew Garrett (2015). Ancestry-constrained phylogenetic analysis supports the Indo-European steppe hypothesis. Language.
lphy-05-c1.quote: Qualitative evidence from reconstructed vocabulary and correlations with archaeological data suggest that Indo-European languages originated in the Pontic-Caspian steppe and spread together with cultural innovations associated with pastoralism
lphy-05-c1.claim: To its supporters, qualitative evidence from reconstructed vocabulary, together with correlations with archaeology, suggests that Indo-European began on the Pontic-Caspian steppe and spread with cultural innovations associated with pastoralism, beginning about 6,500–5,500 years ago.

lphy-05-c1.text: Wolfgang Haak, Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, Nadin Rohland, Swapan Mallick, et al., David Reich (2015). Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe. Nature.
lphy-05-c1.quote: which proposes that early Indo-European speakers were pastoralists of the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian Seas, and that their languages spread into Europe after the invention of wheeled vehicles
lphy-05-c1.claim: The steppe hypothesis proposes that early Indo-European speakers were pastoralists of the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian Seas, and that their languages spread into Europe after the invention of wheeled vehicles.

lphy-05-c1.text: Remco Bouckaert, Philippe Lemey, Michael Dunn, Simon J. Greenhill, Alexander V. Alekseyenko, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray, Marc A. Suchard, Quentin D. Atkinson (2012). Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family. Science.
lphy-05-c1.quote: putative early borrowings between Indo-European and the Uralic language family of northern Eurasia
lphy-05-c1.claim: A second line of argument points to possible early borrowings between Indo-European and the Uralic family of northern Eurasia.

lphy-05-c1.text: Remco Bouckaert, Philippe Lemey, Michael Dunn, Simon J. Greenhill, Alexander V. Alekseyenko, Alexei J. Drummond, Russell D. Gray, Marc A. Suchard, Quentin D. Atkinson (2012). Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family. Science.
lphy-05-c1.quote: However, the reliability of inferences derived from linguistic paleontology and claimed borrowings remain controversial
lphy-05-c1.claim: Critics reply that the reliability of these inferences remains controversial

lphy-05-c2.text: Wolfgang Haak, Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, Nadin Rohland, Swapan Mallick, et al., David Reich (2015). Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe. Nature.
lphy-05-c2.quote: We generated genome-wide data from 69 Europeans who lived between 8,000–3,000 years ago by enriching ancient DNA libraries for a target set of almost 400,000 polymorphisms.
lphy-05-c2.claim: In 2015 a team led by Wolfgang Haak, Iosif Lazaridis and David Reich published genome-wide data from 69 Europeans who lived between 8,000 and 3,000 years ago, enriching their ancient DNA for a target set of almost 400,000 genetic positions.

lphy-05-c2.text: Wolfgang Haak, Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, Nadin Rohland, Swapan Mallick, et al., David Reich (2015). Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe. Nature.
lphy-05-c2.quote: Western and Eastern Europe came into contact 4,500 years ago, as the Late Neolithic Corded Ware people from Germany traced 75% of their ancestry to the Yamnaya
lphy-05-c2.claim: Then, about 4,500 years ago, the Late Neolithic Corded Ware people of Germany traced about 75% of their ancestry to the Yamnaya steppe herders, whose own ancestry combined eastern European hunter-gatherers with a population of Near Eastern ancestry.

lphy-05-c2.text: Wolfgang Haak, Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, Nadin Rohland, Swapan Mallick, et al., David Reich (2015). Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe. Nature.
lphy-05-c2.quote: Although the findings from ancient DNA are silent on the question of the languages spoken by preliterate populations, they do carry evidence about processes of migration which are invoked by theories on Indo-European language dispersals.
lphy-05-c2.claim: The authors themselves noted that ancient DNA is silent on the languages spoken by preliterate populations; it carries evidence only about the migrations that theories of language spread invoke.

lphy-05-c2.text: Wolfgang Haak, Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, Nadin Rohland, Swapan Mallick, et al., David Reich (2015). Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe. Nature.
lphy-05-c2.quote: We caution that the sampled Yamnaya individuals from Samara might not be directly ancestral to Corded Ware individuals from Germany.
lphy-05-c2.claim: They also cautioned that the Yamnaya individuals they sampled, from Samara, might not be directly ancestral to the German Corded Ware.

lphy-05-c3.text: Paul Heggarty, Cormac Anderson, Matthew Scarborough, Benedict King, Remco Bouckaert, et al (2023). Language trees with sampled ancestors support a hybrid model for the origin of Indo-European languages. Science (New York, N.Y.).
lphy-05-c3.quote: Although this date is not consistent with the Steppe hypothesis, it does not rule out an initial homeland south of the Caucasus, with a subsequent branch northward onto the steppe and then across Europe.
lphy-05-c3.claim: That date is not consistent with the steppe hypothesis, but they argued it does not rule out a first homeland south of the Caucasus, with a later branch moving north onto the steppe and from there across Europe.

lphy-05-c3.text: Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, David Anthony, Leonid Vyazov, et al., David Reich (2025). The genetic origin of the Indo-Europeans. Nature.
lphy-05-c3.quote: The Yamnaya archaeological complex appeared around 3300 BCE across the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas, and by 3000 BCE reached its maximal extent from Hungary in the west to Kazakhstan in the east.
lphy-05-c3.claim: The Yamnaya culture appeared around 3300 BC on the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas and by 3000 BC stretched from Hungary to Kazakhstan.

lphy-05-c3.text: Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, David Anthony, Leonid Vyazov, et al., David Reich (2025). The genetic origin of the Indo-Europeans. Nature.
lphy-05-c3.quote: CLV people contributed four-fifths of the ancestry of the Yamnaya, and, entering Anatolia likely from the east, at least a tenth of the ancestry of Bronze Age Central Anatolians, where Hittite was spoken
lphy-05-c3.claim: The same population contributed at least a tenth of the ancestry of Bronze Age central Anatolians, among whom Hittite was spoken.

lphy-05-c3.text: Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, David Anthony, Leonid Vyazov, et al., David Reich (2025). The genetic origin of the Indo-Europeans. Nature.

lphy-07-c1.text: Mark Pagel, Quentin D. Atkinson, Andrew Meade (2007). Frequency of word-use predicts rates of lexical evolution throughout Indo-European history. Nature.
